text: Suppose you'd like to work with a project on GitHub, but you don't have write access to the project. What can you do to contribute?

options.text: Fork the project's repository to your GitHub account, clone the forked repository to your local machine, push changes to your repository, and submit a pull request to the target (upstream) repository.
options.why: GitHub provides forking functionality designed to allow you to work with projects where you aren't an owner or don't have write access. Forking makes a remote copy of the project in your repository that you can then clone locally. To submit updates to the target repository (upstream repository), you can submit a pull request.

options.text: Clone the project to your local machine and push updates directly to the project repository.
options.why: You can't push updates to a repository unless you're the owner or have write access.

options.text: Use git commands to make a copy of the project so that you can work locally. Submit an issue to get your changes into the target repository.
options.why: Although you can clone the target repository to your local machine, you won't be able to push any changes back to it without write access. That's why GitHub provides forking functionality. Although you could submit an issue to the project's repository, using GitHub's fork workflow provides a much better way to contribute to a project.

takeaway: GitHub provides forking functionality designed to allow you to work with projects where you aren't an owner or don't have write access. Forking makes a remote copy of the project in your repository that you can then clone locally. To submit updates to the target repository (upstream repository), you can submit a pull request.

text: In which scenarios should you NOT use GitHub Packages?

options.text: When I want to share code between methods of my application.
options.why: Sharing code within your project is done through code constructs and design patterns.

options.text: When I want to share container images among developers of your team.
options.why: GitHub Packages allow you to easily share container images with the same permissions as your GitHub repository.

options.text: When I want to publish a small code library as an open-source project.
options.why: GitHub packages allow you to publish your libraries in public, and is free for public repositories.

takeaway: Sharing code within your project is done through code constructs and design patterns.

text: When pulling an image to your local environment, which credentials are needed?

options.text: Your GitHub username and a Personal Access Token
options.why: GitHub Packages use your GitHub identity to authenticate you.

options.text: The name of the organization and an API Key
options.why: While you can share packages only within your organization, you need to use your GitHub identity to log in.

options.text: The name of the package and a package key
options.why: Accessing packages and container images is tied to your GitHub account, and not to a specific package.

takeaway: GitHub Packages use your GitHub identity to authenticate you.

text: How can you authenticate to GitHub Packages from your local development environment?

options.why: API Keys can't be used to authenticate with your package manager.

options.text: With my GitHub Credentials (username and password)
options.why: Your GitHub Credentials can't be used to authenticate with your package manager.
Yes, with your GitHub username and a Personal Access Token.

takeaway: Yes, with your GitHub username and a Personal Access Token.
